source_span: the Dallas Fed trimmed mean 6M inflation never really broached 2.5% SAAR and is back down to 2.35%... outstanding Treasury notes and bonds are up 6.8% Y/Y, Fed holdings are up 0.7%
source_chain: Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole tone should mean near-certain odds of a hike, therefore the market's 68% probability (vs. the ~95% typical two weeks out) is oddly low because Warsh ducked the credibility fight with Treasury/government, therefore real doubt remains; underlying inflation is already near target (Dallas Fed trimmed mean 2.35%, core PCE 3.5%) and incoming data (ISM, JOLTS) is softening, therefore the Fed has room to hold; separately, rising yields reflect Treasury supply normalizing after Fed suppression (debt +6.8% Y/Y vs. Fed holdings +0.7%), not fiscal credit risk, so yields alone don't force a hike. Invalidation: August CPI, released 9/11, 'will be the final word for this meeting' — the author's own call is that Warsh finds a way to hold.
pulse_chain: Hike odds ran from 27% to 69% (with GS at 66%, JPM at 58%) while yields broke to multi-year/multi-decade highs in three countries, therefore the market has priced the hike as near-certain; the hold case — attributed to Goldman, citing soft expected core inflation and the Dallas Fed trimmed mean at 2.35% — is dismissed as merely an argument about what the Fed 'should' do, therefore it doesn't bind, because the bond market clears on Treasury supply (debt +6.8% vs. Fed holdings +0.7%) 'no matter which way Warsh votes.' Invalidation: JPMorgan's Sept 11 CPI as the decisive print, with a second consecutive negative payroll print as the out.
why: The Dallas Fed trimmed mean / Treasury-supply hold argument is TS Lombard's (Steven Blitz's) case, not Goldman's, and the pulse misattributes it to Goldman while also inverting its role from 'why yields are normalizing regardless of Fed credit risk' into 'why the bond market ignores Warsh's vote' — a mechanism the note doesn't argue.
